newsitem.title: YEMEN: Singapore wins $187 mln deal to develop Aden port.
newsitem.headline: Singapore wins $187 mln deal to develop Aden port.

text.p: Yemen has awarded Singapore's ports authority a $187 million deal to build quays and a container terminal for a planned free zone at its southern port of Aden, a cabinet minister said on Thursday.
Planning and Development Minister Abdul-Qader Bagammal told reporters the contract would be signed in London on June 17 to help restore the port as a key staging post between Europe and Asia.
Bechtel International Inc and other leading firms competed for the deal.
The project is an important element of the Aden Free Zone, a $580 million project to make Yemen's economic and commercial capital a major transhipment hub in two phases.
"We will try hard to have the first quay operational at the Aden Free Zone by September 1998," Bagammal said.
The zone will have six quays and a 16 metre-deep navigational channel, increased from 12 metres, with all services and facilities to accommodate the world's largest container vessels.

The Aden project is being driven by the Yemeni Investment and Development Company (YEMINCO), an international consortium which includes Saudi investors of Yemeni origin, as well as Saudi and U.S. development firms.
Meneren Corporation of the U.S. is in charge.
The first phase covering dredging and other operations would end by July while piers and the cargo terminal would be ready by April 1999 at a cost of $250 million, Bagammal said.
Aden aims to offer facilities and fast turnaround for the largest carriers now plying routes from Europe through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea to Southeast Asia, Australia and the Far East.
Aden's revival is a challenge to regional rivals -- Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Jeddah and the Gulf ports of Dubai and Jebel Ali in the United Arab Emirates, which are shallower.

Aden was once an important staging post for shipping between Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia. Some 7,000 vessels called each year during the 1950s ad 1960s but war and political uncertainty drove trade elsewhere.
